# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is an established, effective therapy for the prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD) in selected high-risk patients [1]. For decades, transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs) were the standard of care, but they require placement of one or more leads in or on the heart, an approach associated with serious complications including pneumothorax, cardiac perforation, systemic infection, and lead dysfunction [2]. At 10 years post-implant, the risk of lead failure can be as high as 25% in patients with a transvenous ICD. The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed as a totally extravascular alternative to overcome these lead-related complications [3].

## Development and Early Evidence

The feasibility of an entirely subcutaneous defibrillation system was first demonstrated by Bardy and colleagues. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators prevent sudden death from cardiac causes in selected patients but require the use of transvenous lead systems; to eliminate the need for venous access, an entirely subcutaneous ICD system was designed and tested. In small, nonrandomized studies, the device consistently detected and converted ventricular fibrillation induced during electrophysiological testing, and successfully detected and treated all 12 episodes of spontaneous, sustained ventricular tachyarrhythmia. [4] Subsequent pivotal investigational and pooled analyses confirmed safety and efficacy [5,6], and registry data accumulated rapidly.

The EFFORTLESS registry provided important real-world evidence. In a diverse S-ICD registry population, spontaneous shock efficacy was consistently high over 5 years, and very few patients underwent S-ICD replacement with a transvenous device for pacing indications. [7] Early adoption in the United States was characterized in national registry data [8]. Importantly, early cohorts differed from typical ICD populations: patients in previous S-ICD studies had fewer comorbidities, had less left ventricular dysfunction, and received more inappropriate shocks than in typical transvenous ICD trials. [9]

## Pivotal Randomized Evidence

The PRAETORIAN trial was the first randomized comparison in a non-selected ICD population. It was a noninferiority trial in which patients who required an ICD but did not need pacing were randomly assigned to receive either an S-ICD or a TV-ICD; the primary endpoint was a composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks, and the study involved 849 patients (426 in the subcutaneous group and 423 in the transvenous group). [10] The results showed that among patients with an indication for ICD therapy but not for pacing therapy, the subcutaneous ICD was noninferior to the transvenous ICD with respect to the cumulative incidence of the primary end point. [11] A prespecified secondary analysis evaluated the full complication profile [12], and the long-term PRAETORIAN-XL trial is examining whether the S-ICD is superior to the TV-ICD for device-related complications at 8-year follow-up [13].

The UNTOUCHED trial addressed performance in a higher-risk population. It was designed to evaluate the inappropriate shock rate in a more typical, contemporary ICD population implanted with the S-ICD using standardized programming and enhanced discrimination algorithms, and enrolled primary prevention patients with left ventricular ejection fraction ≤35% and no pacing indications. [14] The ATLAS trial enrolled younger or higher-risk patients [15] and demonstrated a clear safety advantage: a composite of lead-related outcomes occurred in one S-ICD patient versus 12 transvenous ICD patients by 6 months, a 92% relative reduction. [16] A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized and propensity-matched studies has further synthesized comparative outcomes [17].

## Programming, Implant Technique, and Defibrillation Testing

Inappropriate shocks, predominantly from cardiac oversensing, were an early limitation; improved sensing algorithms and standardized programming have reduced these events [9,14]. Implant technique has also evolved, including two-incision and intermuscular generator placement [18]. The PRAETORIAN score was developed to estimate the risk of defibrillation failure from device and lead positioning on chest radiographs [19]. The randomized PRAETORIAN-DFT trial then evaluated whether score-based assessment could replace routine defibrillation testing. The trial included 965 patients undergoing de novo S-ICD implantation in 37 centers in Europe, the USA, and Israel, randomized 1:1 to defibrillation testing or no testing with calculation of the PRAETORIAN score. [20] A PRAETORIAN score of <90 serves as a reliable indicator for defibrillation test success, and a score of ≥90 is a strong predictor for failure. [21] Quality-of-life data from comparative trials indicate good early device acceptance [22], although the larger S-ICD generator and pocket-related pain remain practical considerations [23].

## Patient Selection and Guidelines

S-ICD therapy is appropriate for patients who need defibrillation but do not require bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization, or antitachycardia pacing [10,24]. It is particularly attractive for younger patients, those with channelopathies, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, prior device infection, or limited vascular access [25,26]. Outcomes in older patients have also been examined in registry analyses [27]. Comparative meta-analyses consistently show fewer lead-related complications with the S-ICD, at the cost of a somewhat higher inappropriate-shock burden in older device generations [28]. Current US and European guidelines incorporate the S-ICD as a recommended option in appropriately selected patients [11,29].

## Future Directions

A principal limitation of the S-ICD is the inability to provide long-term pacing or antitachycardia pacing. The modular cardiac rhythm management concept pairs a leadless pacemaker in wireless communication with an S-ICD. In the MODULAR ATP trial, the leadless pacemaker in wireless communication with a subcutaneous ICD exceeded performance goals for freedom from major complications, for device-to-device communication, and for acceptable pacing thresholds at 6 months. [30] Such integrated leadless systems may ultimately extend extravascular therapy to patients who also require pacing, broadening the role of the S-ICD in SCD prevention.
